rationale: A wins because it found the sharpest editor-worthy story in the facts: "Replit will tell you it builds working apps — it won't tell you how often they actually work." That is the launch-day pressure point. B sees the same issue but buries it as homework — "Reliability is undisclosed, and it is the first question every reporter on all three beats will ask" — which is where strong angles go to die politely.
gaps_in_A: "You pay per build" invents the pricing unit. The facts say usage-based pricing on top of subscriptions, not per build.
"from one English sentence" overstates the supplied fact. The update says plain-English description, not a one-sentence prompt.
"Replit is betting class on it" is too cute and slightly ahead of the evidence. The education fact is about platform usage, not agent classroom adoption.
Repeated "end-to-end" language brushes the cliché blacklist. It is directionally accurate here, but lazy phrasing still dulls the angle.
gaps_in_B: It misses the best kept angle: reliability. "Reliability is undisclosed" belongs as a contrarian story, not just a proof requirement and uncomfortable question.
"Replit built its name teaching people to code" is not in the update. Heavy education usage does not prove the company's identity or original positioning.
"Replit bets its next users will never write a line of code" adds a growth-market claim the facts do not supply.
"charges for the work, not the seat" smuggles in a seat-pricing contrast. The facts only say usage-based pricing layered on subscriptions.
